title: An Analysis of Financial Literacy Curriculum in Ontario Secondary Education
text_snippet: An Analysis of Financial Literacy Curriculum in Ontario Secondary Education This paper critically examines the development of financial literacy education in Ontario’s secondary curriculum, focusing on its integration into mathematics. Using a critical discourse analysis approach, we trace the historical and political forces shaping financial literacy education since its formal introduction in 2010. We analyze policy documents, curriculum changes, and ideological influences, highlighting how financial literacy has been framed primarily as a tool for individual financial responsibility rather than systemic economic understanding. Our findings reveal a shift from broader conceptions of financial literacy—including equity, ethics, and citizenship—toward a narrower, transactional approach emphasizing personal financial management. We argue that while the inclusion of financial literacy in mathematics has increased its visibility, its current framing limits opportunities for critical engagement with economic systems. We propose a reframing of financial literacy expectations that emphasizes authenticity, mathematical connections, and citizenship to foster a more socially aware and inclusive financial education.

title: Book Review: Creativity, Society, and the Role of Socially Engaged Art in Higher Arts Education
text_snippet: Book Review: Creativity, Society, and the Role of Socially Engaged Art in Higher Arts Education This book review examines Creativity, Society, and the Role of Socially Engaged Art in Higher Arts Education by Kai Lehikoinen. The review considers the book’s central argument that socially engaged art should be recognised as a pedagogical and epistemic field within higher arts education rather than treated as a peripheral form of service. It discusses the book’s major conceptual contributions, its relevance to arts education, and its strengths in linking artistic practice, institutional responsibility, and social engagement. The review also reflects on several areas where the argument could be developed further for readers in arts education.

journal_name: Brock Education: a Journal of Educational Research and Practice
title: Participation or Performance? A Young Person’s Critical Reflections on 'Take Our Kids to Work Day' And Reconceptualization Through a Child Rights Lens
text_snippet: Participation or Performance? A Young Person’s Critical Reflections on 'Take Our Kids to Work Day' And Reconceptualization Through a Child Rights Lens Canada’s national ‘Take Our Kids to Work Day’ (TKWD) initiative celebrated its 30th anniversary in 2023. The annual event allows Grade 9 students across the country an opportunity to learn workplace skills in lieu of their attending classes. This conceptual paper explores how this initiative intersects with child rights and child welfare and includes the critical reflections and the active voice and participation of a youth co-author who participated in TKWD by working at child welfare organization. While presenting the strengths of this initiative, we explore the ways in which young people are viewed as objects of educational policy versus active participants, and agents in their own learning. In (re)conceptualizing this initiative through a child right’s lens, we argue young people must be active participants who fully understand their workplace rights to fully participate in TKWD.

title: Relational Practices and School Climate: An Ethnographic Study in TDSB High Schools
text_snippet: Relational Practices and School Climate: An Ethnographic Study in TDSB High Schools Abstract This ethnographic study explores how relational practices such as inclusive communication, peer support, interdepartmental cooperation, and leadership visibility influence school climate and culture across six high schools within the Toronto District School Board (TDSB). Drawing from the unique dual perspective of the researcher, an Assistant Professor and certified occasional teacher, the study provides situated observations collected over a two-month period in the 2024–2025 school year. The findings are based on anecdotal field notes gathered during regular teaching assignments in varied school contexts, including inner-city and affluent schools with diverse student populations. Thematic analysis revealed three central themes: inclusive communication and trust-building, peer support and informal collaboration, and shared leadership through interdepartmental cooperation. Visibility and relational leadership from school administration were positively correlated with school-wide engagement and student well-being, while their absence often aligned with lower morale and cohesion. title: Educating Cities: An Analysis of 47 Experiences Highlighted by the IAEC in Light of the Public Policy Cycle and the Principles of the Charter of Educating Cities
text_snippet: Educating Cities: An Analysis of 47 Experiences Highlighted by the IAEC in Light of the Public Policy Cycle and the Principles of the Charter of Educating Cities The concept of educative cities acknowledges that education transcends school boundaries, permeating the urban space and involving multiple social actors. The International Association of Educating Cities (IAEC) promotes and documents transformative initiatives worldwide. This article aims to analyze 47 experiences highlighted by the IAEC, focusing on implemented actions, mobilized principles, challenges encountered, and results achieved, based on the public policy cycle framework. This is a qualitative-quantitative, exploratory and descriptive study based on content analysis of documents published by the IAEC. The cases were analyzed according to the Educating Cities Charter principles and the five stages of the public policy cycle. Findings reveal strong adherence to principles such as lifelong learning, cultural access, and democratic citizenship. Civil society organizations and educational institutions played a key role in implementation. However, themes like sustainability, social responsibility, and citizen participation remain underrepresented. title: “Someone Invested in Me”: Learning Through High School Co-operative Education
text_snippet: “Someone Invested in Me”: Learning Through High School Co-operative Education Co-operative education is a type of work-based education in which senior high school students are placed in supervised workplace settings and gain credits towards a graduation diploma. The purpose of this retrospective research was to examine how learning occurs in co-operative education workplaces and the role of co-workers in facilitating student learning. The conceptual framework guiding this research consisted of three theories: Billet’s (2014) theory of mimesis, Munby et al.’s (2003) theory of metacognitive routines, and Snyder’s (2000) hope theory. Three former high school students (one with an IEP and two at risk of dropping out) who had been in automotive co-operative education placements participated in semi-structured interviews. The results showed that the participants valued the skills that were taught in the workplace, and learning involved co-workers who provided individual instruction consisting of observing, imitating, and receiving feedback. title: Indigenous Knowledge and Lifelong Learning: Towards a Decolonial Framework for Epistemic Justice in South Africa
text_snippet: Indigenous Knowledge and Lifelong Learning: Towards a Decolonial Framework for Epistemic Justice in South Africa Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) remain marginalised in mainstream education despite their potential to enrich lifelong learning pathways and strengthen cultural identity. This conceptual paper argues for a decolonial framework that repositions IKS as central to educational design across the lifespan, from early childhood through adult and community learning. Drawing on decolonial theory, Ubuntu pedagogy, and critical Indigenous scholarship, the paper explores how Indigenous epistemologies can foster self-directed learning, intergenerational knowledge transfer, and resilience in marginalised communities. A systematic reading of scholarship on IKS integration highlights persistent barriers: policy centralisation, Western epistemic dominance, and insufficient teacher preparation. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a three-dimensional framework for decolonial lifelong learning: (1) Epistemic Inclusion, embedding IKS as valid and legitimate knowledge; (2) Pedagogical Plurality, incorporating land-based, oral, and spiritual ways of knowing alongside formal schooling; and (3) Community Co-creation, positioning elders and local practitioners as co-educators. title: Online Higher Education for Indigenous Students: Between Digital Colonization and Opportunity
text_snippet: Online Higher Education for Indigenous Students: Between Digital Colonization and Opportunity Online higher education is often framed as a flexible and equitable pathway for expanding access to postsecondary learning. For Indigenous students, however, digital learning environments exist at the intersection of opportunity and ongoing colonial harm. This literature review critically examines research published since 2014 on Indigenous participation and experiences in online higher education across North America and Australia. Guided by Indigenous sovereignty, relational accountability, and digital divide theory, the review synthesizes findings related to infrastructure and access, cultural and pedagogical alignment, psychological and social dimensions of learning, and evidence-based practices for Indigenous-centered online course design. The literature reveals that dominant online learning models frequently reproduce Eurocentric assumptions that marginalize Indigenous epistemologies, contributing to reduced sense of belonging, lower persistence, and widened achievement gaps. title: Go Buya as a Tool for Culturally-Sustaining Pedagogy in Indigenous and Borderland Education
text_snippet: Go Buya as a Tool for Culturally-Sustaining Pedagogy in Indigenous and Borderland Education Indigenous lifelong learning is based on passing down knowledge between generations, maintaining cultural traditions, and education connected to specific places. In the borderland area of Entikong, Indonesia, Indigenous Dayak communities face systemic obstacles to getting an education that respects their culture. They often come across curricula that overlook their heritage. This study presents Go Buya, a game-based learning tool created with the help of local elders, educators, and cultural practitioners to connect traditional knowledge with formal education. Grounded in a culturally sustaining teaching approach, Go Buya weaves Dayak stories, symbols, and civic issues into the gameplay. This promotes student engagement, affirms identity, and encourages critical thoughts about civic duties. Using a Design and Development Research methodology, the project took place in three stages: community consultation, game design, and classroom testing in three borderland schools. The results showed an increase in student curiosity, intergenerational conversations, and collaborative learning, which are essential parts of Indigenous lifelong learning. journal_name: Brock Education: a Journal of Educational Research and Practice
title: Preservice Early-Grade Teachers' Perception of Play-Based Learning in Mathematics Education
text_snippet: Preservice Early-Grade Teachers' Perception of Play-Based Learning in Mathematics Education The study examines preservice early-grade teachers' perceptions of play-based learning (PBL) in teaching mathematics, focusing on its effectiveness and alignment with curriculum demands. Using a cross-sectional survey, data were collected from 150 preservice teachers in Ghana’s Upper West Region through a structured questionnaire. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney U) were conducted via SPSS. Findings reveal that preservice teachers view PBL as beneficial for engagement and conceptual understanding but face challenges in balancing it with structured curricula. Educational level influences perceptions, while sex does not. The study highlights the need for structured PBL integration in teacher education programs.

title: Do Rez Dogs Dream of Chat GPT?
text_snippet: Do Rez Dogs Dream of Chat GPT? Mimi (she/her), a socially awkward Nehiyaw undergraduate student, has an active online life but struggles to connect with her peers in real life (irl), eventually training GenAI to mimic her unattainable crush. This simulacra is the most prominent relationship in Mimi's life until she forms a bond with Lenore (she/they), the resident Elder at Indigenous Student Services, over their shared IndigiGoth subculture. Lenore helps Mimi consider the risks of immersing too deeply in technology, and encourages her to instead take the risks required to connect with others in order to cultivate a more balanced and rewarding life. Then, Mimi unwittingly participates in the rescue of a tech-savvy rez dog, finding unexpected connection and community throughout the process.

title: Biology Graduate School Pathways for Inuit Students and Lessons Learned by Southern Academics
text_snippet: Biology Graduate School Pathways for Inuit Students and Lessons Learned by Southern Academics The minimum requirement for admission to a master's program is normally the successful completion of an undergraduate or baccalaureate degree in an honours program or the equivalent from a recognized university. Inuk student Bryan Vandenbrink is an exception to these expectations. Here, in a loosely autobiographical format, Bryan tells his education story from early high school in Iqaluktuuttiaq through to completing an MSc at the University of Guelph. Co-authors Thomas McIlwraith and Shoshanah Jacobs add short reflections on the journey and identify barriers to post-secondary education for Indigenous students and how those barriers can be reduced.

title: Threads of Indigenous Pedagogy
text_snippet: Threads of Indigenous Pedagogy Mandatory Indigenous education courses in teacher education have a large task to fill by asking to fit in a millennia’s worth of knowledge into a 13-week course, also using a western colonial approach to teaching it as well. Looking at the research in this field of mandatory Indigenous education courses, studies have found a large gap in teacher’s knowledges, understandings, and pedagogies, to teach Indigenous history, pedagogies, and knowledges’ in the classroom. This work will look at how Indigenous pedagogies and specifically eight threads of Indigenous pedagogy can help support preservice educators in learning about Indigenous education and how they can teach Indigenous eduction in their future classrooms.

journal_name: Brock Education: a Journal of Educational Research and Practice
title: Disconnect Between Learning about Indigenous Peoples and Application in the Classroom: Pre-Service Teachers Self-Reported Efficacy
text_snippet: Disconnect Between Learning about Indigenous Peoples and Application in the Classroom: Pre-Service Teachers Self-Reported Efficacy Teacher education programs have taken the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s Calls to Action seriously (TRC, 2015), with many adding a mandatory Indigenous education course to their programs as well as weaving Indigenous knowledges into other courses. Still, there appears to be a disconnect between learning about Indigenous Peoples and integrating this knowledge into the classroom. This study examines the self-reported efficacy of pre-service teachers’ understandings and application of Indigenous knowledges at various stages in their program. Drawing upon a decolonizing theoretical approach and mixed methods methodology, data from a survey and personal autoethnographies are utilized to shed light upon the disconnect. Findings indicate that while the mandatory Indigenous education course led to an increase in efficacy, the explicit weaving of Indigenous knowledges in other courses needs to be made visible. The lack of time to both decolonize pre-service teacher thinking and consider how this knowledge can be applied in the classroom, points to the necessity of an additional Indigenous education course as part of teacher education programming.

title: Learning with the Land: A Case Study of Land-based Education at Batchewana First Nation
text_snippet: Learning with the Land: A Case Study of Land-based Education at Batchewana First Nation This article presents a case study on the impacts of land-based education on Anishinaabe learners, as enacted by the GlenOak Academy SOAR Program within Batchewana First Nation. Grounded in Critical Indigenous Theory (CIT) and guided by participatory action research (PAR) and Storywork methodologies, this research explores how community-led education rooted in Anishinaabe knowledge systems fosters cultural resurgence and educational self-determination. The study was guided by two central questions: How does community-led, land-based education empower Anishinaabe learners to embody traditional knowledge vital for cultural survival? In what ways does cultural engagement through land-based practices facilitate knowledge production and sharing among Anishinaabe students? Findings suggest that land-based education grounded in Anishinaabe philosophies offers a transformative learning experience for Anishinaabe learners. Indigenous and non-Indigenous educators who participated in pedagogical talking circles described the land-based curriculum not only as a means of instruction but as a living dialogue between learners, community knowledge holders, and the land itself. title: Ethical Relationality in Land-based Practices: Braiding Stories, Land, and Spirit
text_snippet: Ethical Relationality in Land-based Practices: Braiding Stories, Land, and Spirit The purpose of this study was to learn from a Tsuut’ina Elders' perspective of land-based learning, teaching, and educational practices and how Tsuut’ina ninisha (way of life) should be recognized as an equal and legitimate way to educate Tsuut’ina children and youth within Tsuut’ina Nation schools. The primary research question is: What does land-based learning mean to Tsuut'ina Elders? Indigenous Métissage creates a space for braiding and weaving boundary crossing, funds of knowledge, and Tsuut'ina ninisha in a respectful, reciprocal, and relational way, where educators become responsible for creating relevant and meaningful curricula. Using Indigenous Métissage as a research praxis to braid and weave Tsuut’ina Elders’ stories, western theories of funds of knowledge and boundary crossing, and personal experiences as an Indigenous educator to find ways of validating Tsuut’ina ninisha as a respected, honoured way of knowing, being, and learning within Tsuut’ina Nation schools. title: Words from Elders in the academic context: Explorations of learning
text_snippet: Words from Elders in the academic context: Explorations of learning Mi’kmaw Elder Albert Marshall defines Etuaptmumk or “Two-Eyed Seeing” as “learning to see from one eye with the strengths of Indigenous ways of knowing and from the other eye with the strengths of Western ways of knowing and to using both of these eyes together, for the benefit of all” (Bartlett, Marshall, & Marshall, 335). This process of collaboration has come to us through a deep understanding and the relationship that Marshall has with his original language. The notion of decolonization now exists in many parts of Canada within academic and community and is employed prevalently within all areas of academia (Daniels et al., 2018; Kerr & Parent, 2018). In discourses of allyship and treaty responsibility, Etuaptmumk is often transmuted into a principle of cooperation and goodwill among those engaged in treaty education advancement and allied service delivery. However, Etuaptmumk’s conceptualization doesn’t fully establish how these competing visions —two-eyed seeing— can coexist in a human being. title: Experimenting with Digital Pedagogical Inquiry Research:
text_snippet: Experimenting with Digital Pedagogical Inquiry Research: Early childhood educator co-researchers and a pedagogist-researcher think together about the processes of collaboration created with a pedagogical inquiry project rooted in pandemic times. We detail our imperfect practices of creating digital methods of pedagogical documentation that emerged in response to COVID-19 policies that bounded our research. Thinking with propositions for practicing slow scholarship and situated improvisations, we grapple with two contradictions that mattered to our work: time and productivity, and writing and dialoguing. Through theoretical provocations and educator re-visitings, we offer practices toward thinking digital pedagogical documentation as an unfamiliar and fraught, but deeply generative and collective-building, ongoing project.

title: Racial Realism in Canadian Teacher Education: The Potential of Cross-Racial Critical Professional Mentorship
text_snippet: Racial Realism in Canadian Teacher Education: The Potential of Cross-Racial Critical Professional Mentorship Critical professional development (CPD) facilitates creative empowering teacher practice and racial justice accountability. This paper extends United States’ CPD literature through a qualitative critical race analysis of a one-year Canadian teacher education anti-racist cross-racial mentorship project. Focus groups with 13 teacher candidate (TC) members of the project suggest cross-racial CPD mentorship enhanced the TCs’ anti-racist 1) experiences with their teacher education program, 2) engagement with conversations, and 3) pedagogical comprehension. A fourth finding revealed the TCs recognized their lack of comprehension regarding whiteness and a desire to learn more. Through a critical race theory racial realist lens, the findings suggest practical ways in which Canadian anti-racist teacher educators can contribute to the democratic racial equity and decolonization commitments of education systems.

title: Reclaiming Relational Pedagogies: The Role of Talking Circles in Decolonizing Higher Education Classrooms
text_snippet: Reclaiming Relational Pedagogies: The Role of Talking Circles in Decolonizing Higher Education Classrooms This article explores the use of Talking Circles as a decolonizing pedagogical practice within higher education, grounded in Indigenous epistemologies and relational worldviews. Drawing on the works of Indigenous scholars such as Graveline, Wilson, Archibald, and Simpson, the article positions Talking Circles not merely as instructional strategies but as ceremonial, spirit-centered pedagogies that resist the Eurocentric hierarchical and individualistic norms of Western academia. Through autoethnographic reflection and student narratives from undergraduate and graduate education courses, the article demonstrates how Talking Circles foster relational accountability, ethical engagement, and transformative learning. By centering oral tradition, reciprocity, and communal learning, Talking Circles reconfigure the classroom as a space of collective inquiry and healing. The article also addresses the ethical considerations of integrating culturally grounded practices within institutional contexts, emphasizing the importance of protocol, consent, and community accountability. title: Designing a MOOC Learning Environment embedded with Gamifications to Enhance Higher Order Thinking
text_snippet: Designing a MOOC Learning Environment embedded with Gamifications to Enhance Higher Order Thinking This study presents the design and development of a MOOC learning environment embedded with gamification elements aimed at enhancing higher-order thinking skills. The research adopts a design and development approach, utilising the ADDIE and ASSURE instructional design models. The study provides a comprehensive background and rationale for each component of the design process, highlighting the theoretical foundations that support the integration of gamification into the MOOC environment. Theories such as the Mechanics, Dynamics, and Emotions (MDE) framework for gamification are integrated into the learning activities to promote engagement and motivation. Additionally, elements of Online Collaborative Learning (OCL) are incorporated to facilitate interactive and social learning experiences, while the selected MOOCs reflect the principles of Connectivism, emphasising the networked nature of knowledge. A thorough analysis of these theories informs the design elements aimed at promoting cognitive development among learners. title: Investigating Public School Language Initiatives in Northern Manitoba
text_snippet: Investigating Public School Language Initiatives in Northern Manitoba An emergent imperative in public school priorities across Canada in recent years is that of Indigenous education. An important part of this imperative, as articulated by Indigenous peoples and educational authorities, is that of Indigenous language programming. In response, some public-school districts have explored and initiated Indigenous language programs. The purpose of this study was to investigate how public-school districts have navigated and managed Indigenous language programming in northern Manitoba – one of some regions in Canada for which Indigenous language use is comparatively high. Participation was solicited from public school districts in this region that have initiated Indigenous language programming. Interviews with school administrators and educators were conducted to explore how the programs were developed, implemented and the impact they have had upon students, families, and communities. This study found that public schools in northern Manitoba have experienced some success in recent years with their respective language programming in spite of difficulties such as the availability of qualified teachers, resource procurement, and legislative limitations. title: Reinvigorating the Notion of Becoming “Scholars Before Researchers”: Experiences With Systematic Literature Reviews
text_snippet: Reinvigorating the Notion of Becoming “Scholars Before Researchers”: Experiences With Systematic Literature Reviews Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) present scholars with an opportunity to develop deep conceptual and methodological understanding of their field of interest. Unfortunately, this skill is not necessarily a compulsory component of one’s formal graduate training. In this paper, we have storied our lived experiences with SLRs in the form of 13 vignettes. These vignettes were created from a series of open-ended questions that were developed from continued engagement with 10 articles, which were foundational in our own teaching and learning of the SLR method. A content analysis of the vignettes revealed five inter-related themes: (1) Rigor, (2) Process, (3) Benefits, (4) Learning, and (5) Teaching. Each of these five themes are discussed in relation to recollections of our experiences with SLRs. We provide recommendations for engagement with the SLR method with the goal of empowering researchers, professors, and students to explore its use in postsecondary coursework and research activities.

title: (u)Mzantsi Classics: Dialogues in Decolonisation from Southern Africa
text_snippet: (u)Mzantsi Classics: Dialogues in Decolonisation from Southern Africa Using a dialectical framework, this book interrogates the role that classics has played in southern Africa (Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and especially South Africa) from diverse perspectives, from the earliest European colonizers to the Fallist protests of 2015/2016. While (u)Mzantsi Classics is grounded in the historical and contemporary realities of the African south, Canadian readers will find many parallels with the vital issues confronting our own universities today. Both candid and hopeful, this book makes a compelling case for the role that classics can play in helping us to understand and navigate an increasingly polarized world.

journal_name: Brock Education: a Journal of Educational Research and Practice
title: Editorial
text_snippet: Editorial This issue represents my first as Editor-in-Chief of Brock Education. It is an honour to fill this role at a time in which the academic world is in great turmoil, in Canada and across the globe. Our daily newsfeeds are filled with stories of direct and indirect challenges to academic freedom, freedom of speech, EDID (Equity, Diversity, Inclusion, and Decolonization), student mobility, funding of institutions, and intra- and extramural research. As scholars, we need to be conscious of the noise of those who seek to undermine education and hinder scholarship and knowledge mobilization. We need to focus on those aspects of our lives as teachers, researchers, and leaders that will allow us to reinforce the foundations of learning and teaching across the lifespan while maintaining our own well-being.

journal_name: Brock Education: a Journal of Educational Research and Practice
title: A Transgender Teacher’s Pre-Service Experience
text_snippet: A Transgender Teacher’s Pre-Service Experience This qualitative, single-subject case study examines a transgender pre-service teacher’s experiences completing an educator preparation program (EPP) in a predominantly rural region in the southeast United States. The purpose of this case study is to describe and understand a transgender pre-service teacher’s experiences in finding and completing the field experience requirements across multiple school districts. Stories of the participant’s experiences, university faculty members’ accounts, and communication documents inform the research. Results demonstrate obstacles the preservice teacher faced during their field placement and hindrances to securing employment post-graduation. Implications for further research are discussed.

title: Silenced Professoriate
text_snippet: Silenced Professoriate This paper examines the significant pressures reshaping the contemporary professoriate, particularly the erosion of academic freedom in higher education. The study conducted qualitative interviews with tenured faculty from two Southern Ontario universities to explore how fiscal constraints, administrative overreach, peer dynamics, and technological disruptions (such as generative artificial intelligence) impact faculty roles. Findings reveal that universities are increasingly adopting managerial models prioritizing efficiency and performance metrics over independent intellectual inquiry, a trend participants identified more than a decade ago. This shift, driven by chronic fiscal shortfalls, constrains faculty members’ ability to serve as public intellectuals and undermines universities’ critical societal role. The paper argues that reversing this trend requires structural reforms within universities, including reducing administrative burdens, securing stable public funding, and fostering a culture that values intellectual debate and dissent. title: Mental Health in Ontario Sexuality Education
text_snippet: Mental Health in Ontario Sexuality Education This article engages in a content analysis of the Ontario Health and Physical Education Grades 1-8 and 9-12 curriculum documents to better understand if, when, and how mental health is discussed within Ontario provincial health education curriculum documents. Accordingly, this article provides an overview of both historically and currently how mental health as a construct has been addressed within Ontario health education curricula. Following, the article provides recommendations of how improved conversations regarding mental health through both consent-oriented and trauma-informed practices could take place in Ontario health education curriculum documents and classes.

title: Beyond Work: AI and Educational Labour
text_snippet: Beyond Work: AI and Educational Labour The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has prompted significant reflection on the nature of work and labour among teachers and students. This essay examines the implications of AI on educational labour, highlighting the distinction between work, encompassing unpaid and broader educational contributions, and labour, defined by economic metrics. AI’s capability to perform educational tasks raises concerns about its potential to replace certain aspects of teaching while emphasizing its limitations in fostering genuine educational experiences. The discussion explores how AI may transform schooling and education, reshaping roles and responsibilities, and addressing broader socio-economic and technological dynamics. Ultimately, this analysis considers the future of work in education amidst the evolving presence of AI.Keywords: Educational labour, work and labour dichotomy, post-work society, AI and educational reform
